The Section on Detailed Exposition (Paṭiniddesavāra) – Analysis 15
The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Requisites.
Therein, what is the mode of conveying requisites?
It is: "Those phenomena which produce this phenomenon."
Whatever phenomenon generates another phenomenon, that is its requisite.
What is the characteristic of a requisite?
A requisite has the characteristic of generating.
Two things produce [results]: the cause (hetu) and the condition (paccaya).
In this regard, what is the characteristic of the cause, and what is the characteristic of the condition?
The cause has the characteristic of being specific (asādhāraṇa), while the condition has the characteristic of being general (sādhāraṇa).
How might this be? Just as, for the production of a sprout, the seed is the specific cause while the earth and water are common causes;
for the earth and water are the conditions (paccaya) for the sprout, whereas the seed is its intrinsic nature (sabhāva-hetu).
Or just as when milk is poured into a jar it becomes curd, yet there is no simultaneous coexistence of the milk and the curd;
even so, there is no simultaneous coexistence of the cause and the condition.
For this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) has arisen with a cause and with conditions.
For it has been said: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises. Thus is the entire dependent origination.
In this way, ignorance is the cause of ignorance, and improper attention is its condition.
Previous ignorance is the cause of subsequent ignorance.
In this context, the former ignorance is the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) of ignorance, while the latter ignorance is the active manifestation (*paryavasthāna*) of ignorance;
the former underlying tendency serves as the cause for the nourishment of the latter manifestation, by way of being its immediately preceding cause,
just like a seed is to a sprout.
However, that wherein the fruit is produced is its cause by way of being a remote cause (*paramparahetu*).
For cause is twofold: the immediately preceding cause (*samanantarahetu*) and the remote cause. Thus, ignorance also has a twofold cause: the immediately preceding cause and the remote cause.

Or alternatively, just as the bowl, the wick, and the oil are conditions for a lamp but not its intrinsic cause—since it is impossible to light a lamp with a bowl, a wick, and oil without fire—they are merely its conditions.
Intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is the cause, like a lamp.
Thus, intrinsic nature is the cause and extrinsic nature (parabhāva) is the condition.
The internal is the cause; the external is the condition.
The producer is the cause (*hetu*); the grasper is the condition (*paccaya*).
The unique is the cause; the common is the condition.
The meaning of continuity is the sense of non-interruption; the meaning of production is the sense of fruit; the meaning of rebirth-linking is the sense of renewed existence.
The meaning of obstruction is the meaning of obsession; the meaning of non-eradication is the meaning of latent tendency; the meaning of non-penetration is the meaning of ignorance;
the meaning of non-full-understanding is the meaning of the seed of consciousness.
Where there is no cutting off, there is continuity; where there is continuity, there is rebirth; where there is rebirth...
In that case, where there is fruit, there is rebirth-linking; where there is rebirth-linking, there is renewed existence;
where there is renewed existence, there is an impediment; where there is an impediment, there is obsession;
where there is obsession, there is non-eradication.
Where there is non-eradication, there is underlying tendency; where there is underlying tendency, there is non-penetration; where there is non-penetration, there is ignorance;
where there is ignorance, there is consciousness accompanied by taints that is not fully understood;
where there is consciousness accompanied by taints that is not fully understood, there is the state of being a seed.

The aggregate of virtue is a condition for the aggregate of concentration; the aggregate of concentration is a condition for the aggregate of wisdom; the aggregate of wisdom is a condition for the aggregate of liberation; the aggregate of liberation is a condition for the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Knowledge of the ford is a condition for knowledge of the drink; knowledge of the drink is a condition for knowledge of the bowl; knowledge of the bowl is a condition for knowledge of oneself.
Or, just as visual consciousness arises dependent upon the eye and visible forms.
In this context, the eye is a condition by way of being a dominant condition; visible forms are a condition by way of being an object-condition;
light is a condition by way of providing a basis; and attention is the cause as the intrinsic nature.
Formations are a condition for consciousness, being the cause as the intrinsic nature.
Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form; its own nature is the cause.
Name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases; its own nature is the cause.
The six sense bases are the condition for contact; their own nature is the cause.
Contact is the condition for feeling; its own nature is the cause.
Feeling is the condition for craving; its own nature is the cause.
Craving is the condition for clinging; its own nature is the cause.
Clinging is the condition for becoming; its own nature is the cause.
Becoming is the condition for birth; its own nature is the cause.
Birth is the condition for aging and death; its own nature is the cause.
Old age and death are the condition for sorrow; their intrinsic nature is the cause.
Sorrow is the condition for lamentation; its intrinsic nature is the cause.
Lamentation is the condition for suffering; its intrinsic nature is the cause.
Suffering is the condition for mental grief; its own nature is the cause.
Mental grief is the condition for despair; its own nature is the cause.
Thus, whatever is a decisive support (*upanissaya*), all that is an accessory (*parikkhāra*).
Therefore the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "Those phenomena which produce that phenomenon.
The Mode of Conveying Requisites is concluded.
